passages.text: Targeting of tripartite neuron-cancer-immune cell crosstalk augments response to chemotherapy and immunotherapy
Summary

We report presence of cholinergic nerve fibers in the periphery and stroma of colon cancer tissues and their correlation with poor T cell and increased macrophage infiltration. <sentence_start/>We employed hydrogel-mediated localized delivery of an FDA-approved local anesthetic, bupivacaine (BUP), to target acetylcholine (ACh)-mediated crosstalk of cholinergic neurons with cancer and immune cells. <sentence_start/>Localized BUP-Gel therapy promotes T cell-mediated tumor inhibition and enhances the antitumor response of systemic chemotherapy and immunotherapy. <sentence_start/>Further, blockade of cancer- and immune cell-specific ACh receptors inhibits tumor growth, alters the TME, and augments the impact of chemotherapy and immunotherapy. <sentence_start/>Finally, we demonstrate that ACh receptor antagonists polarize macrophages toward an M1-like phenotype and activate T cell immunity in tumor explants of patients. <sentence_start/>Therefore, targeting cholinergic signals through localized delivery of anesthetics, as well as direct immune reprogramming via cholinergic receptor antagonists, may provide a means to modulate this tripartite crosstalk, with potential implications for therapeutic strategies.

Highlights
Cholinergic neurons are associated with immunosuppression in patients with colon cancer
Acetylcholine suppresses cytotoxic T cell activity and M1 macrophage polarization
Local anesthetics and receptor antagonists activate antitumor T cell immunity
Targeting cholinergic signaling enhances chemotherapy and immunotherapy responses

Jain et al. identify cholinergic nerve-derived acetylcholine as a mediator of immunosuppression in colon cancer and show that localized hydrogel-based delivery of local anesthetics and pharmacological blockade of acetylcholine receptors activate anti-tumor immune responses and enhance the efficacy of chemotherapy and immunotherapy.
Introduction

Cancer cells sculpt their local microenvironment by utilizing growth signals and modulating host cells for their progression.<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cub.2020.06.081" pmid="32810447" pmcid="PMC8194051" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This complex tumor microenvironment (TME) features immune cells, stromal cells, blood vessels, and extracellular matrix that coordinates with cancer cells, supporting their survival, growth, and spread.<citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2023.02.016" pmid="36917948" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The interactions within TME, particularly between immune cells and cancer cells, create an immunosuppressive TME that diminishes the immune cell-mediated killing of cancer cells, thereby accelerating the tumor growth.<citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-018-0014-x" pmid="29686425" pmcid="PMC5998822" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Tumor innervation has emerged as a key hallmark of cancer progression, where innervating neurons facilitate immunosuppression along with cancer progression and metastasis.<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41568-019-0237-2" pmid="31974491" pmcid="PMC7709871" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2023.02.012" pmid="36917953" pmcid="PMC10202656" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation> Tumor innervation is evident in solid tumors, including prostate, gastric, pancreatic, oral, breast, and skin,<citation rid="bib6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/scitranslmed.3009569" pmcid="PMC4374618" pmid="25143365" count="1"><sup>6</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-024-07767-5" pmid="39112700" pmcid="PMC11633843" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2017.11.007" pmid="29249692" pmcid="PMC5760435" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-022-05374-w" pmid="36323780" pmcid="PMC9646485" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.canlet.2024.216986" pmid="38797233" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation> and the density of these nerve fibers has been associated with cancer-related pain and poor clinical outcomes.<citation rid="bib11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fba.2021-00147" pmid="35664834" pmcid="PMC9164247" count="1"><sup>11</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fba.2021-00046" pmid="34632313" pmcid="PMC8493966" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation> Neurons interact with cancer cells and other stromal cells, including immune cells in the TME primarily through neurotrophic factors, neuropeptides, and neurotransmitters that remodel the TME,<citation rid="bib11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fba.2021-00147" pmid="35664834" pmcid="PMC9164247" count="1"><sup>11</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fba.2021-00046" pmid="34632313" pmcid="PMC8493966" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation> thereby making it a promising therapeutic target for cancer treatment.<citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41573-024-01017-z" pmid="39242781" pmcid="PMC12123372" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation>

Within the autonomic nervous system, sympathetic nerves contribute to tumor progression by releasing noradrenaline, which activates β-adrenergic receptors on cancer and stromal cells, thereby enhancing proliferation, angiogenesis, and immunosuppression.<citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-022-05374-w" pmid="36323780" pmcid="PMC9646485" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.can-10-0522" pmid="20823155" pmcid="PMC2940980" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.aah5072" pmid="29051371" pmcid="PMC5783182" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This adrenergic signaling also impairs CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell function and promotes infiltration of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs).<citation rid="bib16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00262-018-2243-8" pmid="30229289" pmcid="PMC6326964" count="1"><sup>16</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/jci129502" pmid="31566578" pmcid="PMC6877316" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>As a result, β-blockers are now being explored in clinical trials to inhibit adrenergic signaling in combination with conventional cancer therapies.<citation rid="bib18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/2162402X.2023.2284486" pmcid="PMC10732641" pmid="38126031" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Cholinergic signals from parasympathetic fibers promote tumor growth and metastasis via muscarinic receptor activation on cancer cells in prostate and gastric cancers, which upregulate nerve growth factor (NGF) and enhance parasympathetic nerve survival and function.<citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-024-07767-5" pmid="39112700" pmcid="PMC11633843" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2016.11.005" pmid="27989802" pmcid="PMC5225031" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In contrast, cholinergic signaling suppresses progression and stemness in pancreatic cancer.<citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.cd-18-0046" pmid="30185628" pmcid="PMC6214763" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>However, the role of cholinergic signaling in regulating immunosuppression in colon cancer is not known.

In addition to the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, highly complex and specialized enteric neurons present in the colon are organized as Meissner’s plexus and Auerbach’s plexus.<citation rid="bib21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms21093391" pmcid="PMC7247003" pmid="32403316" count="1"><sup>21</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Acetylcholine (ACh), one of the primary neurotransmitters released by these enteric neurons, maintains homeostasis in the colon.<citation rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2020/8024171" pmcid="PMC7495222" pmid="32963521" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>ACh maintains colonic homeostasis through interacting with specific muscarinic ACh and nicotinic ACh receptors (mAChR and nAChRs) that are known to be differentially expressed on different cell types.<citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.suronc.2019.09.003" pmid="31536927" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers14092322" pmid="35565451" pmcid="PMC9100020" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation> While cholinergic fibers releasing ACh are normally present in the muscularis propria as part of the enteric nervous system, their role in colon cancer progression and in the immunosuppressive TME is not known. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we hypothesize that ACh release from cholinergic neurons might play a critical role in tumor progression and its TME.

The effects of neurons can be targeted by either preventing neurotransmitter release or by blocking the signaling events initiated by the neurotransmitters.<citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41573-024-01017-z" pmid="39242781" pmcid="PMC12123372" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Local anesthetics, such as bupivacaine (BUP) and lidocaine, can impede the propagation of action potentials, thereby inhibiting the neurotransmitter release.<citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/lra.s154512" pmid="30122981" pmcid="PMC6087022" count="1"><sup>25</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Earlier studies showed that BUP inhibits the progression of breast and lung cancers,<citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.abj5435" pmcid="PMC8494443" pmid="34613777" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2021.616445" pmcid="PMC7991299" pmid="33777755" count="1"><sup>27</sup></citation> while pre-operative peritumoral infiltration of lidocaine enhances disease-free and overall survival in patients with breast cancer.<citation rid="bib28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.01966" pmid="37023374" count="1"><sup>28</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Although earlier studies showed the impact of ACh receptor (mAChR and nAChR) antagonists as therapeutic interventions against many cancers,<citation rid="bib29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/biomedicines7030058" pmid="31405140" pmcid="PMC6783861" count="1"><sup>29</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbadis.2023.166875" pmid="37673358" count="1"><sup>30</sup></citation> the consequences of targeting ACh-releasing nerve fibers or blocking ACh signaling in cancer and immune cells have not been studied. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we hypothesize that targeting ACh signaling or ACh release may suppress tumor growth by obstructing interactions between cholinergic neurons, cancer cells, and immune cells, ultimately modulating the TME. <sentence_start/>In this study, we showed the presence of cholinergic neurons in human colon cancer tissues and their tripartite cross-talk with TAMs and CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells. <sentence_start/>We further demonstrated that targeting this ACh-mediated tripartite cross-talk of cholinergic neurons with cancer cells and immune cells inhibits tumor progression, mitigates immunosuppression, and activates T cell immunity.
Results
Cholinergic nerve fibers are associated with reduced CD8 T cells and increased macrophage infiltration in patients with colon cancer

We used a cohort of 68 patients with colon cancer with distribution with respect to gender (male 40, female 28), location of tumor (47 right sided and 21 left sided) and stages (2 with stage I, 44 with stage II, 16 with stage III, and 6 with stage IV) (Figure 1A, Data S1). <sentence_start/>We stained the colon cancer tissue sections from these patients with neurofilament-L (NEFL), a general neuronal marker, and choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), a specific marker for cholinergic neurons (Figure 1B). <sentence_start/>The number of NEFL/ChAT-positive neurons was quantified in high-power fields (HPF) in tumor-dense and adjoining areas. <sentence_start/>We observed a high density of cholinergic nerve fibers, bundles, or ganglion cells within the tumor stroma and the tumor periphery in 32 of the 68 patients (∼47% of total patients) (Figures 1C-1E, Data S1). <sentence_start/>We further performed Kaplan-Meier survival analysis using the KM-Plotter database and found that concurrent high expression of both NEFL and ChAT is associated with worse overall survival (<italic>p</italic> = 0.0013) but not with recurrence-free survival (<italic>p</italic> = 0.062) (Figures S1A and S1B). <sentence_start/>We next analyzed a publicly available dataset ( ) from patients with primary colorectal cancer and observed that high expression of NEFL and ChAT was associated with poor recurrence-free survival (<italic>p</italic> = 0.019) in early-stage colon cancer (Figure S1C and Data S2). <sentence_start/>Multivariate Cox regression analysis showed a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.64 (95% confidence interval, <italic>p</italic> = 0.02), suggesting that NEFL and ChAT expression may be independent prognostic factors in early stages (Figure S1D and Data S2). <sentence_start/>However, we did not observe a similar level of significance across all stages of colorectal cancer (HR = 1.37, <italic>p</italic> = 0.07), suggesting that NEFL and ChAT expression may be linked to disease progression and may have prognostic utility in early stages of colon cancer.<sentence_start/>Figure 1

Figures S1E and S1F). <sentence_start/>We then assessed infiltration of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells by counting the average number of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells across multiple HPFs and categorizing them as high or low based on a median cut-off in stage II samples (dataset 3). <sentence_start/>We observed low infiltration of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells in intratumoural regions in ∼57% of patients with high NEFL/ChAT expression, whereas there is an increased infiltration of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells in ∼61% of patients with low NEFL/ChAT expression (<italic>p</italic> = 0.0159) (Figures 1I-1K; Figures S1G and S1H). <sentence_start/>To validate these findings, we performed multiplex immunofluorescence analysis on patient samples stratified by high and low NEFL/ChAT expression. <sentence_start/>In samples with high NEFL/ChAT expression, we observed a higher frequency of CD68<sup>+</sup> cells and a lower frequency of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells in regions surrounding nerve structures (Figure 1L). <sentence_start/>In contrast, samples with low NEFL/ChAT expression showed reduced abundance of CD68<sup>+</sup> cells and a higher frequency of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells localized around nerve areas (Figure 1M). <sentence_start/>As ACh is the primary neurotransmitter released by cholinergic nerves, we quantified the ACh in colon cancer tissues using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). <sentence_start/>Notably, we observed a ∼2-fold higher level of ACh (<italic>p</italic> = 0.0032) in colon tumors compared with matched adjacent normal tissues (Figure 1N), suggesting a potential role for ACh in tumor progression. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the presence of cholinergic nerve fibers in colon cancer tissues is associated with increased macrophage recruitment and reduced infiltration of CD8<sup>+</sup> cells, suggesting a potential immunosuppressive role for cholinergic signaling in the TME.
ACh augments cancer cell proliferation

As our investigations on clinical samples revealed a higher incidence of cholinergic neurons and higher levels of ACh in colon tumor tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues, we hypothesized that ACh released by cholinergic nerve fibers may enhance cancer cell proliferation. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we determined the effect of ACh (50 μM) on cancer cell proliferation in a time-dependent manner. <sentence_start/>ACh supplementation led to a ∼1.3-fold increase in the proliferation of CT26 (murine colon cancer cell line) cells at 72 h in comparison to CT26 cells grown in a normal medium (NM) (Figure 2A). <sentence_start/>Similarly, there is a ∼1.1-fold increase in proliferation of 4T1 (murine breast cancer cell line) cells upon ACh supplementation at 72 h (Figure S2A). <sentence_start/>Similar to ACh, feeding of carbachol (an agonist of cholinergic receptors) (50 μM) also led to a ∼1.5-fold increase in the proliferation of CT26 cells and a ∼1.3-fold increase in the proliferation of 4T1 cells. <sentence_start/>(Figure 2B; Figure S2B). <sentence_start/>ACh feeding (50 μM) also led to a ∼1.2-fold increase in the size of CT26 spheroids and a ∼1.3-fold increase in the size of 4T1 spheroids compared to untreated spheroids (Figure 2C; Figure S2C). <sentence_start/>Similarly, feeding of carbachol (50 μM) showed a ∼1.2-fold increase in size of CT26 and 4T1 spheroids compared to untreated spheroids (Figure 2D; Figure S2D). <sentence_start/>Therefore, these results suggest that ACh and carbachol boost cancer cell proliferation, probably via activation of cholinergic receptors.<sentence_start/>Figure 2

BUP inhibits ACh-mediated cell proliferation

To validate the ACh-mediated crosstalk between cholinergic neurons and cancer cells, we employed BUP, an FDA-approved non-opioid, long-acting local anesthetic that blocks sodium and potassium channels on neurons and inhibits action potentials.<citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/lra.s154512" pmid="30122981" pmcid="PMC6087022" count="1"><sup>25</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.abj5435" pmcid="PMC8494443" pmid="34613777" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>We hypothesized that BUP-mediated inhibition of ACh release would disrupt ACh-driven interactions between cholinergic neurons and cancer cells, ultimately reducing cancer cell proliferation. <sentence_start/>To assess the effect of BUP, we first evaluated its cytotoxicity on Neuro2A (N2A) cells, a murine cholinergic neuroblast cell line. <sentence_start/>BUP treatment up to 100 μM did not affect the viability of N2A cells (Figure S2E). <sentence_start/>While BUP treatment did not change the intracellular ACh levels in N2A cells, there is a ∼1.3-fold decrease in extracellular ACh levels (Figure 2E). <sentence_start/>Culture of CT26 cells in the presence of BUP (100 μM)-treated N2A conditioned media (CM (BUP)) showed a ∼1.2-fold decrease in proliferation compared to CT26 cells treated with CM from untreated N2A cells (CM (UT)) (Figures 2F and 2G). <sentence_start/>Further, supplementation of ACh (50 μM) in CM (BUP) led to a ∼1.2-fold increase in cell proliferation (Figures 2F and 2G). <sentence_start/>Similarly, treatment of 4T1 cells with CM (BUP) resulted in a ∼1.3-fold decrease in proliferation, and ACh supplementation led to a ∼1.3-fold increase in proliferation (Figure S2F). <sentence_start/>Supplementation of carbachol (50 μM) also resulted in a ∼1.3- and a ∼1.4-fold increase in proliferation of CT26 and 4T1 cells in comparison to cancer cells that were treated with CM (BUP) (Figure 2H; Figure S2G). <sentence_start/>BUP treatment did not affect the cell viability of CT26 or 4T1 cells till 200 μM (Figures S2H and S2I). <sentence_start/>Supplementation of ACh did not alter the proliferation of BUP-treated N2A cells, suggesting that BUP downregulates ACh levels without affecting the viability or proliferation of N2A cells (Figure S2J). <sentence_start/>Moreover, BUP treatment did not affect the proliferation of N2A, CT26, and 4T1 cells (Figures S2J-S2L). <sentence_start/>In contrast, ACh supplementation increased proliferation by ∼1.2-fold in BUP-treated CT26 and 4T1 cells (Figures S2K and S2L), suggesting that BUP in the CM of N2A-treated cells is not responsible for inhibiting cancer cell proliferation. <sentence_start/>We also quantified ACh levels in CT26 and 4T1 cells treated with BUP and observed ∼4-fold and ∼2-fold decreases in intracellular ACh levels, which may be due to BUP’s non-specific actions (Figures S2M and S2N). <sentence_start/>However, there was no significant change in the released ACh from BUP-treated CT26 and 4T1 cells (Figures S2M and S2N), suggesting that BUP treatment selectively attenuates ACh release in neuronal cells without affecting the extracellular ACh levels in cancer cells.

We next created co-spheroids of CT26 and 4T1 cells with N2A cells at a 9:1 ratio and observed an increase in spheroid size compared to CT26 and 4T1 spheroids alone (Figure 2I; Figure S2O). <sentence_start/>BUP treatment did not affect the spheroid size of CT26 spheroids, whereas BUP-treated co-spheroids (CT26-N2A) showed a ∼1.2-fold decrease compared to untreated co-spheroids (Figure 2I). <sentence_start/>There was a ∼1.2-fold increase in spheroid size upon ACh feeding to BUP-treated co-spheroids compared to only BUP-treated co-spheroids (Figure 2I). <sentence_start/>Similarly, BUP-treated 4T1/N2A co-spheroids showed a ∼1.3-fold decrease in spheroid size compared to untreated 4T1 co-spheroids, and ACh feeding mitigated this effect (Figure S2O). <sentence_start/>Therefore, these results demonstrate that BUP inhibits ACh-mediated crosstalk between cholinergic neurons and cancer cells, thereby inhibiting cancer cell proliferation.
Localized delivery of BUP inhibits tumor progression

As local anesthetics need to be delivered at their action site, and any systemic exposure can cause toxicity,<citation rid="bib31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ams2.265" pmid="29123854" pmcid="PMC5667269" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation> we hypothesize that hydrogel-mediated localized delivery of BUP would be an effective strategy to inhibit the release of ACh from peripheral cholinergic neurons. <sentence_start/>In addition, the hydrogel-mediated sustained release of BUP will provide reduced toxicity compared to carrier-free delivery. <sentence_start/>In our earlier studies, we reported the engineering of a non-immunogenic, lithocholic acid-derived, low-molecular-weight hydrogelator (A13) (Figure 2J).<citation rid="bib32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acscentsci.9b00551" pmid="31660434" pmcid="PMC6813554" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>We demonstrated that A13 hydrogel can entrap a range of chemotherapeutic drugs without altering the physical properties of the gel and allow the sustained and sequential release of a combination of chemotherapeutic drugs.<citation rid="bib32" ref-type="bibr" As the neuro-immuno-cutaneous system releasing ACh is the key component of skin,<citation rid="bib34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/cpr.12677" pmcid="PMC6869210" pmid="31441145" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation> we tested the impact of BUP-Gel on tumor growth kinetics against subcutaneous syngeneic murine colon (CT26), breast (4T1), and melanoma (B16) cancer models, where tumor-bearing mice were either left untreated or treated with a single dose of BUP-Gel (40 mg/kg of BUP). <sentence_start/>Tumor growth kinetics revealed a significantly slower rate of progression on BUP-Gel treatment in CT26 tumors compared to untreated tumors with a ∼2-fold decrease in ACh levels (Figures 2N and 2O). <sentence_start/>Similarly, BUP-Gel-treated 4T1 tumors showed reduced tumor growth kinetics, with a 3.5-fold decrease in ACh levels (Figures 2P and 2Q), suggesting that BUP-Gel inhibits tumor growth, likely by reducing ACh release. <sentence_start/>We validated a similar finding in the B16 tumor model (Figures S2T and S2U). <sentence_start/>To validate that inhibition of ACh is responsible for slow tumor growth kinetics, we prepared an ACh-loaded BUP-Gel (BUP-ACh-Gel) that can release the ACh along with BUP and compared the tumor growth kinetics of BUP-Gel with BUP-ACh-Gel against CT26, 4T1, and B16 tumor models. <sentence_start/>Although BUP-Gel showed a ∼2-fold reduction in tumor growth at day 16, there was a ∼1.7-fold increase in tumor volume upon BUP-ACh-Gel treatment compared to BUP-Gel-treated CT26 tumors (Figure 2R). <sentence_start/>BUP-ACh-Gel also showed a higher tumor growth rate than BUP-Gel in the 4T1 (Figure 2S) and B16 models (Figure S2V). <sentence_start/>Similarly, BUP-Gel loaded with carbachol (BUP-CARB-Gel) enhanced the tumor growth kinetics in CT26 and 4T1 models compared with BUP-Gel (Figures 2T and 2U). <sentence_start/>Therefore, these results suggest that localized delivery of BUP inhibits ACh, thereby mediating tumor growth inhibition.
BUP-Gel therapy alters the immune landscape in tumor tissues

As we observed a correlation of cholinergic neurons with macrophage and T cell infiltration in patients with colon cancer, we investigated the impact of BUP-Gel therapy, which inhibits ACh release, on the tumor immune microenvironment. <sentence_start/>We performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on untreated (UT) and BUP-Gel-treated CT26 tumors using the 10X genomics platform (Figure S3A).<citation rid="bib35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/imm.13783" pmid="38501302" pmcid="PMC7616077" count="1"><sup>35</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Unsupervised clustering of 13,939 QCed cells, obtained from UT and BUP-Gel-treated tumor samples, identified 16 distinct clusters (Figure 3A; Figure S3B). <sentence_start/>We classified the clusters as immune cell clusters (0, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, and 16) and non-immune cell clusters (1, 3, 12, 13, and 15) based on the <italic>Ptprc</italic> expression (Figure 3B). <sentence_start/>The non-immune cells mainly consisted of fibroblasts, cancer cells, and erythrocytes, with clusters 1 and 15 showing higher expression of fibroblast-associated transcripts (Figure 3C) and cluster 12 showing erythrocyte-specific transcripts (Figure 3C). <sentence_start/>Cluster 3 showed high levels of transcripts associated with the cell cycle, such as <italic>Mki67</italic>, <italic>Top2a</italic>, <italic>Pcna</italic>, and <italic>Birc5</italic>, which were classified as proliferating tumor cells (Figure 3C). <sentence_start/>Notably, we observed a reduced proportion of proliferating tumor cells (cluster 3) in BUP-treated tumors compared to UT tumors, supporting that BUP inhibits tumor growth (Figure 3D).Figure 3

To delineate the macrophage heterogeneity, we analyzed the expression of genes associated with M1-like macrophages (<italic>Cd86</italic> and <italic>Tnf)</italic> and M2-like macrophages (<italic>Mrc1</italic> and <italic>Arg1</italic>). <sentence_start/>Cluster 1 showed a distinct M2-like profile with high <italic>Mrc1</italic> and <italic>Arg1</italic>, and cluster 10 displayed high proliferative capacity (<italic>Mki67</italic>) in addition to M2-like features (Figure 3G). <sentence_start/>In contrast, cluster 11 expressed M1-like markers (<italic>Cd86</italic> and <italic>Nos2</italic>); cluster 0 showed a mixed M1/M2 profile (<italic>Nos2</italic>, <italic>Arg1</italic>, and <italic>Mrc1</italic>); and cluster 8 (monocytic MDSCs) expressed <italic>Mrc1</italic>, <italic>Arg1</italic>, and <italic>Cd86</italic>, indicating a hybrid state (Figure 3G). <sentence_start/>Comparison of the expression of M1-like (<italic>Tnf</italic> and <italic>Cd86</italic>) and M2-like (<italic>Arg1</italic> and <italic>Mrc1</italic>) markers across macrophages, MDSCs and monocytic clusters in UT and BUP-treated tumors revealed elevated <italic>Tnf</italic> expression in cluster 11 in BUP-treated tumors, consistent with their M1-like phenotype (Figure 3H). <sentence_start/>Elevated <italic>Tnf</italic> was also observed in clusters 0, 5, and 8 upon BUP treatment (Figure 3H). <sentence_start/><italic>Cd86</italic> expression was found to be increased in M1/M2 hybrid macrophages (cluster 0) and was also high in other populations, including M2-like macrophages (clusters 1 and 10) (Figure 3H). <sentence_start/>In contrast, the expression of M2 marker, <italic>Arg1</italic>, decreased in M2-like macrophages (cluster 1) as well as in MDSCs (cluster 2) upon BUP treatment (Figure 3H). <sentence_start/>Similarly, <italic>Mrc1</italic> expression was reduced in M2-like macrophages (clusters 1), M1-like macrophages (cluster 11), M1/M2 hybrids (cluster 0), and monocytic MDSCs (cluster 8) (Figure 3H). <sentence_start/>We further compared the proportion of cells within myeloid cell clusters in UT and BUP-Gel-treated tumors and observed a reduced proportion of M2-like macrophages (clusters 1 and 10) in BUP-Gel-treated tumors (Figure 3I).

Among T cell populations, <italic>Cd8</italic>-expressing cells (clusters 3, 7, and 9) are identified as cytotoxic T cells, while cluster 12 expressing <italic>Cd4</italic> is classified as a helper T cell cluster (Figure 3J). <sentence_start/>Among CD8<sup>+</sup> subsets, cluster 3 showed elevated expression of cytotoxic markers (<italic>Gzmb</italic>, <italic>Gzmk</italic>, <italic>Prf1</italic>, and <italic>Ifng</italic>) and immune checkpoints (<italic>Pdcd1</italic>, <italic>Havcr2</italic>, and <italic>Ctla4</italic>), indicating an activated phenotype (Figure 3J). <sentence_start/>Cluster 9 also expressed cytotoxic markers and immune checkpoints with additional expression of <italic>Mki67</italic>, suggesting proliferative capacity (Figure 3J). <sentence_start/>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells in cluster 12 expressed high <italic>Ctla4</italic>, and NK cells (cluster 4) exhibited expression of <italic>Gzmb</italic> and <italic>Prf1</italic> (Figure 3J). <sentence_start/>BUP treatment led to an increase in CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells (clusters 3 and 9) and a reduction in <italic>Ctla4</italic>-expressing CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells (cluster 12) (Figure 3K). <sentence_start/>Comparison of cytotoxic marker and immune checkpoint expression across T cell clusters revealed that <italic>Gzmk</italic> was upregulated in CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells (clusters 3 and 9) following BUP treatment (Figure 3L), while <italic>Ctla4</italic> expression was decreased across all T cell clusters in BUP-treated tumors (Figure 3M). <sentence_start/>Collectively, these findings suggest that BUP modulates the TME by shifting the tumor-associated myeloid compartment toward an M1-like phenotype and enhancing cytotoxic T cell activity, thereby contributing to immune activation and anti-tumor immune responses.

To validate the effect of ACh on macrophage polarization, we converted murine bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) into M1-like phenotype using LPS and IFN-γ followed by ACh (50 μM) treatment (Figure 4E; Figure S4B). <sentence_start/>ACh treatment led to a ∼1.1-fold decrease in iNOS<sup>+</sup> cells with a ∼1.6-fold decrease in iNOS MFI (mean fluorescence intensity) in comparison to untreated M1-like BMDMs, suggesting the suppressive role of ACh on M1 polarization (Figure 4F). <sentence_start/>To further validate the ACh-mediated neuron-macrophage interactions, we treated BMDMs with conditioned media of untreated (CM-UT) and BUP-treated N2A cells (CM-BUP) and examined the <italic>Nos2</italic> and <italic>Arg1</italic> expression by quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) (Table S1). <sentence_start/>BMDMs treated with CM (UT) exhibited a ∼1.7-fold increase in <italic>Arg1</italic> expression compared to untreated BMDMs, while CM (BUP) treatment displayed a >3-fold decrease in <italic>Arg1</italic> expression compared with CM (UT)-treated BMDMs (Figure 4G). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, BMDMs treated with CM (BUP) showed a ∼2-fold increase in <italic>Nos2</italic> expression in comparison to BMDMs treated with CM (UT) (Figure 4G). <sentence_start/>Further, we treated M1-like BMDMs with CM (UT) and CM (BUP) and evaluated iNOS expression by flow cytometry (Figure 4H). <sentence_start/>CM (BUP) treatment led to a ∼2-fold increase in iNOS MFI in comparison to M1-like BMDMs treated with CM(UT), whereas iNOS expression was reversed upon treatment of M1-like BMDMs with ACh-supplemented CM(BUP) (Figure 4I). <sentence_start/>Therefore, consistent with our scRNA-seq results, these findings suggest that inhibiting ACh-mediated signaling promotes the polarization toward an M1-like macrophage phenotype.
Localized BUP-Gel therapy activates the cytotoxic T cell response

pmcid="PMC9792152" count="1"><sup>37</sup></citation> we profiled the T cells for cytotoxic markers using flow cytometry in CT26 tumors treated with BUP-Gel and BUP-ACh-Gel (Figure S4C). <sentence_start/>BUP-Gel treatment led to a >25-fold increase in IFN-γ<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells compared to untreated CT26 tumors (Figure 4J). <sentence_start/>However, ACh abrogated this effect and caused a >8-fold decrease in IFN-γ<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells (Figure 4J). <sentence_start/>We observed a ∼7.5-fold increase in TNF-α<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells in BUP-Gel-treated tumors compared to untreated tumors, and ACh mitigated this effect (Figure 4K). <sentence_start/>We next assessed the co-expression of granzyme B with cytokines IFN-γ and TNF-α in CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells and observed a marked increase in CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells co-expressing IFN-γ and TNF-α, granzyme B and TNF-α, as well as granzyme B, IFN-γ, and TNF-α upon BUP-Gel treatment, and ACh abrogated this effect (Figures 4L and 4M). <sentence_start/>Recent studies have shown that CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells, like CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells, exert cytotoxic functions by releasing granzymes and effector cytokines, often in response to viral infections and cancer.<citation rid="bib38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.immuni.2021.11.015" pmid="34910940" pmcid="PMC8809482" count="1"><sup>38</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Our results showed a ∼7-fold increase in IFN-γ<sup>+</sup>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells compared to untreated CT26 tumors, and ACh abrogated this effect (Figure S4D). <sentence_start/>We also observed a ∼13-fold increase in TNF-α<sup>+</sup>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells in BUP-Gel-treated tumors, and ACh feeding decreased it by ∼3.5-fold (Figure S4E). <sentence_start/>Analysis of exhaustion markers (PD1, TIM3, and CTLA4) on T cells revealed that BUP-Gel treatment resulted in a ∼2-fold decrease in PD1<sup>+</sup>TIM3<sup>-</sup> CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells, with no significant change in PD1<sup>+</sup>TIM3<sup>+</sup> CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells, and a ∼5-fold increase in CTLA4<sup>+</sup> CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells compared to untreated cells (Figures S4F-S4H). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, ACh further enhanced the expression of exhaustion markers, increasing PD1<sup>+</sup>TIM3<sup>-</sup> and PD1<sup>+</sup>TIM3<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells, as well as CTLA4<sup>+</sup> CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells, suggesting that ACh not only suppresses cytotoxic markers but also promotes T cell exhaustion, thereby keeping a check on the T cell To validate the ACh-mediated effect on T cell cytotoxicity, we stimulated mouse splenic CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells and treated them with ACh (150 μM) (Figure 4N; Figure S4I). <sentence_start/>ACh treatment led to a ∼1.6-fold decrease in MFI of granzyme B and a ∼1.4-fold decrease in the MFI of IFN-γ compared to untreated CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells (Figures 4O and 4P). <sentence_start/>We further investigated ACh-mediated neuron-T cell interactions, where stimulated T cells were treated with conditioned media from untreated (CM-UT) or BUP-treated (CM-BUP) N2A cells (Figure 4Q). <sentence_start/>We observed a ∼1.5-fold increase in IFN-γ MFI in CM(BUP) treated CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells compared to CM (UT) treated T cells, which decreased in ACh-supplemented CM (BUP) treated CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells (Figure 4R). <sentence_start/>These results indicate that ACh-mediated signaling suppresses cytotoxic T cell responses, and its inhibition enhances T cell activation.

Next, to delineate the impact of CD4 and CD8 T cells, we depleted CD4<sup>+</sup> and CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells in BUP-Gel-treated CT26 tumor-bearing mice to assess tumor inhibition. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, depletion of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells abrogated the effect of BUP-Gel therapy on tumor volume (Figure 4S; Figure S4J). <sentence_start/>However, we did not observe any change in tumor volume upon CD4<sup>+</sup> T cell depletion. <sentence_start/>Therefore, although BUP-Gel therapy induces both CD8<sup>+</sup> and CD4<sup>+</sup> cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), the magnitude of cytolytic activity of CD8<sup>+</sup> CTLs is markedly superior to that of the CD4<sup>+</sup> CTLs. <sentence_start/>This does not exclude the meaningful contributions of CD4<sup>+</sup> CTLs and other immune effector cells in building an effective anti-tumor immune network when treated with BUP-Gel. <sentence_start/>We also investigated the effect of BUP-Gel therapy in immunocompromised mice (NSG) using the CT26 tumor model and did not observe any change in tumor growth compared to BALB/c mice (Figure S4K).

We next assessed central memory and effector memory T cells in the peripheral blood of mice bearing CT26 tumors to determine the impact of BUP-Gel on these memory T cell subsets (Figure S4L). <sentence_start/>BUP-Gel treatment led to ∼2.5-fold increase in central memory T cells and ∼1.5-fold increase in effector memory T cells (Figures S4M and S4N). <sentence_start/>To investigate the effect of BUP-Gel on long-term memory T cells, we resected CT26 tumors at 50 mm<sup>3</sup> and treated the resection site with BUP-Gel. <sentence_start/>We observed that 3 out of 8 mice did not show tumor recurrence. <sentence_start/>After 20 days of BUP-Gel treatment, we rechallenged these three mice with CT26 cells and observed a ∼4-fold slower rate of tumor growth compared to naive untreated mice at day 36 (Figure S4O). <sentence_start/>Upon assessing long-term memory cells in peripheral blood at day 36, we observed a >3.5-fold increase in central memory CD8 T cells in BUP-Gel-treated tumors, without any change in effector memory T cells, compared to untreated tumors (Figures S4P and S4Q).

Since we employed hydrogel-mediated delivery of BUP to delineate changes in the immune microenvironment, we investigated whether BUP-Gel offers advantages over the direct tumor-site (BUP-TS) injection of BUP without hydrogel. <sentence_start/>We observed that BUP-TS did not significantly affect tumor progression (Figure 4T). <sentence_start/>Although BUP-TS did not induce any change in IFN-γ<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells and TNF-α<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells, there was a similar decrease in MFI of ARG1 within macrophages (Figures 4U and 4V; Figure S4R). <sentence_start/>Therefore, these results suggest that BUP-Gel outperforms BUP-TS in inhibiting tumor growth and modulating the TME, primarily due to the sustained release of BUP from A13 gel.

Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy, including anti-PD1/anti-PD-L1 and anti-CTLA4 (aCTLA4), has gained attention for cancer treatment despite its low response rates.<citation rid="bib43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1500596" pmid="26028255" pmcid="PMC4481136" count="1"><sup>43</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>As BUP-Gel therapy enhances the activation of T cells along with CTLA4 expression on T cells, we hypothesized that localized BUP-Gel treatment might enhance the efficacy of aCTLA4 therapy. <sentence_start/>The combination of BUP-Gel and aCTLA4 showed ∼1.8-fold reduction of tumor growth in comparison to aCTLA4-treated tumors and a >4-fold decrease in tumor growth when compared with untreated B16 tumors (Figure 5I). <sentence_start/>Flow cytometric quantification of T Cells showed a ∼3.5-fold increase in granzyme B<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells, a ∼1.5-fold increase in IFN-γ<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T Cells, a ∼3-fold increase in IFN-γ<sup>+</sup>CD4<sup>+</sup> T Cells and a ∼1.7-fold increase in TNF-α<sup>+</sup>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells in tumors treated with the combination of BUP-Gel and anti-CTLA4 compared to untreated tumors (Figures 5J-5M). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, treatment with BUP-Gel and anti-CTLA4 also led to increased frequency of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells co-expressing IFN-γ and TNF-α as well as granzyme B and IFN-γ compared to untreated tumors (Figures 5N and 5O).

Adoptive T cell transfer (ACT) uses tumor-reactive T cells that are expanded <italic>ex vivo</italic> and reinfused into patients to boost T cell-mediated killing of cancer cells.<citation rid="bib44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.21037/atm-22-6196" pmid="36660664" pmcid="PMC9843349" count="1"><sup>44</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>We employed OT-I T cells, which are reactive toward OVA-peptide-expressing B16 cells, in combination with localized BUP-Gel therapy against the B16-OVA tumor model. <sentence_start/>The combination of BUP-Gel with OT-I T cells showed a ∼4-fold and ∼8-fold reduction of tumor growth in comparison to OT-I T cell transfer alone and untreated tumors (Figure 5P). <sentence_start/>Flow cytometry revealed a ∼1.6-fold increase in granzyme B<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells with a ∼1.3-fold increase in MFI, a ∼5-fold increase in IFN-γ<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells, and a ∼1.4-fold increase in MFI of TNFα in CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells upon treatment with the combination of BUP-Gel and OT-I T cells (Figures 5Q-5T). <sentence_start/>We observed enhanced frequency of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells co-expressing IFN-γ and TNF-α, granzyme B and TNF-α as well as all co-expression of granzyme B, IFN-γ, and TNF-α in BUP-Gel and OT-I treated tumors (Figures 5U and 5V). <sentence_start/>Analysis of BUP-Gel therapy in combination with OX, aCTLA4, and ACT showed additive effects on tumor regression (Table S2), suggesting that the combination therapy acts through independent, non-redundant pathways. <sentence_start/>Overall, these results suggest that localized BUP-Gel therapy can be combined with existing chemotherapy and immunotherapy regimens to achieve better efficacy and clinical outcomes.

ACh mediate signals through specific muscarinic and nicotinic ACh receptors (mAChRs and nAChRs), and these receptors are known to be expressed differentially on different cell types (Table S3).<citation rid="bib45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/2398212818820506" pmcid="PMC7058246" pmid="32166177" count="1"><sup>45</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Therefore, we analyzed a publicly available colorectal cancer dataset and identified 15 distinct clusters using unsupervised clustering.<citation rid="bib46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2020.03.048" pmid="32302573" count="1"><sup>46</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>We determined receptor expression across different clusters (Figures 6A-6D), and identified that malignant cells, macrophages, and T cells express mAChRs, <italic>CHRM3</italic>, and <italic>CHRM5</italic> (Figures 6B and 6D), whereas among nAChRs, <italic>CHRNA7</italic>, and <italic>CHRNB1</italic> are expressed by malignant cells, M1-like macrophages, and CD8<sup>+</sup> T effector cells (Figures 6C and 6D). <sentence_start/>We next stratified patient tumors into high vs. low mAChR and nAChR expression and found that tumors with high mAChR expression exhibit increased Treg proportions and decreased M1-like macrophages (Figures S6A and S6B). <sentence_start/>In contrast, tumors with high nAChR expression were associated with reduced proportions of M1-like macrophages, accompanied by enrichment of exhausted CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells (Figures S6C and S6D). <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that expression of these receptors may be linked to immunosuppressive cells in the TME.Figure 6

Since immune cells and cancer cells expressed CHRM3, CHRM5, and CHRNA7 in the human scRNA dataset, we tested their protein expression in the CT26 tumor model and observed that these receptors are expressed in cancer cells, macrophages, and T cells within CT26 tumors (Figures S6E-S6G). <sentence_start/>We used specific antagonists to block these receptors and investigated the effect of hydrogel-mediated localized delivery of CHRM3 antagonist (darifenacin) (DARF-Gel), CHRM5 antagonist (ML375) (ML375-Gel), and CHRNA7 antagonist (methyllycaconitine citrate) (MLA-Gel) on CT26 tumor growth. <sentence_start/>Tumor growth kinetics revealed slower progression with all treatments, with >2-fold reductions in final-day tumor volume compared with untreated tumors (Figure 6E). <sentence_start/>Treatment of DARF-Gel, ML375-Gel, and MLA-Gel led to a >2-fold increase in the frequency of CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells compared to untreated tumors (Figure 6F). <sentence_start/>We also observed a >1.5-fold increase in granzyme B<sup>+</sup>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells in tumors treated with these antagonists compared with untreated tumors (Figure 6G). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, we observed a ∼1.3-fold decrease in ARG1<sup>+</sup> macrophages and a ∼2.5-fold decrease in ARG1 MFI in tumors treated with DARF-Gel, ML375-Gel, and MLA-Gel compared to untreated tumors (Figures 6H and 6I). <sentence_start/>To validate these findings, we assessed the effect of blocking ACh receptors on ACh-treated BMDM-derived M1-like macrophages (Figure S6H). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, antagonizing ACh receptors led to ∼1.2-fold increase in iNOS<sup>+</sup> cells compared to ACh-treated M1 macrophages (Figure S6I). <sentence_start/>Similarly, all three antagonists showed >2-fold increase in IFN-γ<sup>+</sup> cells compared to ACh-treated splenic CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells (Figures S6J and S6K).

Discussion

Tumors promote nerve innervation into the tumor niche by secreting neurotrophic factors, facilitating interactions among cancer cells, neurons, and immune cells via neurotransmitters and neuropeptides.<citation rid="bib49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2023.02.002" pmid="37059069" pmcid="PMC10107403" count="1"><sup>49</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This neuron-cancer-immune crosstalk modulates TME and contributes to tumor progression and immunosuppression.<citation rid="bib50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciimmunol.aay9368" pmid="32917793" count="1"><sup>50</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Previous studies demonstrated that the presence of NEFL- and PGP9.5-positive nerves within colon tumors is associated with poor prognosis and reduced overall survival in patients, as corroborated by our Kaplan-Meier survival analysis from publicly available databases.<citation rid="bib51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.modpat.2024.100565" pmid="39025405" count="1"><sup>51</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/cncr.26117" pmid="21480205" count="1"><sup>52</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Moreover, multivariate Cox regression analysis also demonstrated independent prognostic significance of NEFL and ChAT in early stages, revealing probable involvement of cholinergic nerves in the progression of colon cancer independent of clinicopathological features, including age, laterality, and therapy. <sentence_start/>We further demonstrated that ∼47% of patients with colon cancer exhibit high levels of cholinergic neurons (NEFL and ChAT) in tumor tissues, and this is associated with reduced CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell infiltration and increased macrophage accumulation. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, elevated ACh levels in tumor tissues compared with adjacent normal regions suggest active ACh-mediated communication within the TME.

ACh is one of the key neurotransmitters released from enteric nerves in the gastrointestinal tract, crucial for maintaining gut motility.<citation rid="bib53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.brainresbull.2007.02.005" pmid="17452281" count="1"><sup>53</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Although non-neuronal cells, including cancer cells, can secrete ACh at nanomolar concentrations,<citation rid="bib54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/srep40802" pmcid="PMC5244394" pmid="28102288" count="1"><sup>54</sup></citation> these levels are modest and often regulated by local acetylcholinesterase activity.<citation rid="bib55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pharmthera.2018.10.002" pmid="30291908" pmcid="PMC6348061" count="1"><sup>55</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In contrast, neuronal ACh release occurs at substantially higher concentrations, ranging from 0.1 to 1 μM in the central nervous system to transient micromolar levels (10-100 μM) in peripheral nerves to mM concentrations at synaptic junctions.<citation rid="bib56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jnc.15943" pmid="37621094" pmcid="PMC10616967" count="1"><sup>56</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12035-009-8087-7" pmid="19844813" pmcid="PMC2777263" count="1"><sup>57</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This highlights a greater potential of neuronal ACh to modulate TME through ACh signaling. <sentence_start/>To account for the rapid degradation of ACh, we utilised a higher ACh concentration than the intratumoral ACh concentrations detected by LC-MS/MS. <sentence_start/>Neuronal and tuft-cell-derived ACh promotes gastric tumorigenesis,<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2016.11.005" pmid="27989802" pmcid="PMC5225031" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> while cholinergic innervation in prostate cancer promotes tumor growth, invasion, and metastasis.<citation rid="bib58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1236361" pmid="23846904" count="1"><sup>58</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>However, the effect of ACh is organ specific and concentration dependent, as cholinergic signaling has been shown to suppress cancer stem cells and liver metastatic growth in pancreatic cancer.<citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.cd-18-0046" pmid="30185628" pmcid="PMC6214763" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Consistent with this, we demonstrated that ACh enhances cancer cell proliferation in both 2D and 3D culture models and modulates immune cells, suggesting engagement of neuronal ACh within the TME, thereby presenting a potential therapeutic target for local anesthetics.

A recent clinical trial revealed that peritumoral lidocaine (a local anesthetic) injection before surgery significantly improves disease-free and overall survival in patients with breast cancer.<citation rid="bib28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.01966" pmid="37023374" count="1"><sup>28</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Although earlier studies focused on liposomal formulation of local anesthetics like BUP,<citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.abj5435" pmcid="PMC8494443" pmid="34613777" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation> systemic delivery of these drugs can be life threatening.<citation rid="bib31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ams2.265" pmid="29123854" pmcid="PMC5667269" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Therefore, our study utilized a hydrogel-based localized system for slow and sustained release of BUP at the tumor that limits tumor growth more effectively than BUP solution, highlighting the benefit of localized hydrogel-based systems. <sentence_start/>Our A13-gel scaffold was shown to exhibit good biocompatibility, <italic>in vivo</italic> persistence with minimal immune infiltration, and gradual clearance over 21-50 days in rodents.<citation rid="bib32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acscentsci.9b00551" pmid="31660434" pmcid="PMC6813554" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>However, further evaluation of long-term biodegradability, systemic safety, and manufacturing scalability is essential for clinical translation. <sentence_start/>While localized BUP-Gel treatment demonstrated immune activation in tumors, likely by inhibiting neuronal ACh release, BUP can also exert other pleiotropic effects, such as inducing autophagy in lung cancer cells, inducing apoptosis in rhabdomyosarcoma cells, and exerting anti-inflammatory effects in astrocytes.<citation rid="bib27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2021.616445" pmcid="PMC7991299" pmid="33777755" count="1"><sup>27</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12935-015-0229-6" pmid="26225122" pmcid="PMC4518519" count="1"><sup>59</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/ejn.12364" pmid="24083665" pmcid="PMC4211363" count="1"><sup>60</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Moreover, as BUP induces broad neural blockade, the observed anti-tumor and immune regulatory effects may involve the influence of other neurotransmitter-mediated signals beyond cholinergic signals.

Cholinergic activation in macrophages via nAChRs signals suppresses pro-inflammatory responses, possibly through inhibition of NF-κB signaling and reduced TNF and IL-1 production.<citation rid="bib61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature01339" pmid="12508119" count="1"><sup>61</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>ACh released during perineural invasion in pancreatic cancer impairs CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell infiltration, suppresses IFN-γ, and promotes a Th1-to-Th2 immune shift.<citation rid="bib62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.can-19-2689" pmid="32098780" count="1"><sup>62</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In line with this, our results show that inhibiting ACh release using BUP-Gel reprograms macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype and enhances T cell cytotoxicity, which are abrogated by ACh supplementation. <sentence_start/>While these findings highlight the role of cholinergic signaling in immune suppression, the involvement of other neural inputs affected by BUP cannot be ruled out entirely.

Our scRNA-seq analysis in patients with colon cancer revealed predominant CHRM3 expression in malignant cells and macrophages, whereas CHRNA7 and CHRM5 were broadly expressed across immune cell populations. <sentence_start/>CHRM3 signaling has been demonstrated to support tumor growth and suppress anti-tumor immunity.<citation rid="bib63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms24010596" pmid="36614038" pmcid="PMC9820315" count="1"><sup>63</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41389-018-0099-6" pmid="30459304" pmcid="PMC6246593" count="1"><sup>64</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers13133220" pmid="34203220" pmcid="PMC8267754" count="1"><sup>65</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Similarly, CHRNA7 signaling promotes tumor growth in gastric, colon, liver, and pancreatic cancers and suppresses macrophage pro-inflammatory cytokine production by downregulating NF-κB.<citation rid="bib66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.heliyon.2020.e03611" pmcid="PMC7090353" pmid="32215331" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcp.28220" pmid="30701535" count="1"><sup>67</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2119/2008-00079.parrish" pmid="18584048" pmcid="PMC2435495" count="1"><sup>68</sup></citation> Consistent with this, our results demonstrated tumor growth inhibition and improved anti-tumor immunity upon blockade of these receptors. <sentence_start/>In addition to modulating neuron-derived cholinergic signaling, therapeutic targeting of these receptors also reflects the direct effects on immune cells within the TME. <sentence_start/>Therefore, our findings suggest that while BUP-Gel primarily targets neural inputs to the TME by inhibiting ACh release, targeting of ACh receptors represent another parallel and distinct strategy to modulate the TME.

Therefore, in summary, hydrogel-mediated delivery of FDA-approved local anesthetics and cholinergic receptor antagonists can inhibit ACh-mediated tumor progression, reverse ACh-mediated immunosuppression, and augment responses to chemotherapy and immunotherapy.
Limitations of the study

Although several studies have suggested a role for neurons in cancer progression, there is no evidence for the role of acetylcholine from cholinergic neurons in the colon TME. <sentence_start/>However, it is important to consider the following limitations while interpreting the results. <sentence_start/>First, the multivariate Cox regression analysis using the cohort did not adjust for MMR (mismatched repair) status, a crucial prognostic factor in colon cancer, due to the unavailability of data. <sentence_start/>Second, tumor harbors a mixed population of neurons, and BUP causes non-specific neuronal blockade, including cholinergic, sympathetic, sensory, and enteric neurons within the TME. <sentence_start/>While ACh supplementation and ACh receptor blockade indicates the role of cholinergic signaling in tumor growth and immunosuppression, the involvement of each neural input requires further investigation. <sentence_start/>Third, non-neuronal sources of ACh, including cancer cells, stromal cells, and tuft cells, also contribute to the TME, and their individual roles need to be elucidated. <sentence_start/>Fourth, replicating physiological ACh concentrations is challenging, as ACh levels vary across tissues and are rapidly degraded by acetylcholinesterase. <sentence_start/>Lastly, the response to cholinergic receptor blockade in our patient-derived tumor explant studies may be influenced by the baseline immune composition of individual patient tumors, a finding that requires further investigation to better define patient-specific responses. <sentence_start/>In addition, patient-derived tumor explant studies were limited to MLA treatment only and not performed with darifenacin or ML375 due to limited tissue availability.

Publicly available Smartseq2-based single cell RNA sequencing data and associated metadata on colorectal cancer ( ) were downloaded from the TISCH website ( ) and used for analysis with the R (v4.4.0) package Seurat (v5.3.0).<citation rid="bib76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkac959" pmid="36321662" pmcid="PMC9825603" count="1"><sup>76</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2021.04.048" pmid="34062119" pmcid="PMC8238499" count="1"><sup>77</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The data were log-normalized, and highly variable genes were selected for scaling. <sentence_start/>The first twenty principal components were selected to infer cell-cell similarity and construct a shared nearest-neighbor graph. <sentence_start/>Transcriptionally distinct cell populations were identified by unsupervised clustering, and the results were visualized using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP).<citation rid="bib78" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.21105/joss.00861" count="1"><sup>78</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Associated metadata, including sample information and cell-type annotations, were then incorporated into the Seurat object. <sentence_start/>Harmony (v1.2.3) was used to normalize the PCA embeddings across different patient samples.<citation rid="bib79" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41592-019-0619-0" pmid="31740819" pmcid="PMC6884693" count="1"><sup>79</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The RunHarmony function was used with the default parameters to correct batch effects with ‘Sample’ as the batch variable. <sentence_start/>The first twenty harmony dimensions and a resolution of 0.5 were then used with the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions. <sentence_start/>Dimension reduction was performed using the RunUMAP function.
